doc.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Record company relationship and quick studio sessions
summary: Person describes a loose relationship with his small label, budgets, recording a CD in a day or two, and using the best New York players.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Well in your career as a recording musician, we mentioned you’ve recorded some seventy-some albums. Does the economics, has it changed a lot over the years? Trying to get records, out, keeping track of how they’re doing? Has your relationship with record companies changed?

I don’t know. I have a good relationship with my record company, I’ve been there for ages. But I’ve been big and small. And I like small. The economics are different but I still like small because I can keep up with what’s going on, I have control of my own production and if I need something somewhere they get it there immediately so I can keep a hands-on on what’s going on.
To get specific, do they give you X amount of dollars to work with when you make a recording, and then it’s up to you to like keep within a budget?

Yeah some companies do. But mine is so loosely — it’s such a loose relationship there. We go over what we’re going to do and I’ve been doing it so long I know how to do it and do it cost-wise I hope. Well I must be ‘cause I wouldn’t be there.
That’s right. You’d be looking elsewhere.
How long do you usually get to record a CD these days?
I usually go right in and do it in one day, two days. I don’t fool around with them. I go in and get it over with.
You have to have a supporting cast who can keep it— © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Oh I know all my supporting cast, yes, that’s why I can do it. Because in New York you know you’ve got the best, so I always get the best and I work with the best, so that’s it for me.
